title: Module Documentation: Fair Games Theorem
content: The module documentation introduces the Fair Games Theorem (Wiedijk #62), also known as the Optional Stopping Theorem. It establishes the intuitive content: in a fair game (martingale), no betting strategy (stopping time) can change the expected value. The document outlines the mathematical framework (martingales, stopping times, bounded stopping times), the proof approach via Mathlib's submartingale and supermartingale machinery, and historical notes tracing the theorem from Bachelier (1906) through Doob (1953).
mathContext: If $X$ is a martingale and $\tau$ is a bounded stopping time, then $E[X_\tau] = E[X_0]$. This is the mathematical content of Wiedijk's #62: no strategy beats a fair game.

title: isFairGame: Martingale as Fair Game
content: Defines isFairGame as a thin wrapper around MeasureTheory.Martingale from Mathlib. A process f is a fair game with respect to filtration F and measure mu if E[f_{n+1} | F_n] = f_n for all n: the expected future value always equals the current value given all observed information. This is the formal expression of a 'fair game' where no player has a systematic advantage.
mathContext: A process $f : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a martingale (fair game) if it is adapted to $\mathcal{F}$, each $f_n$ is integrable, and $E[f_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] = f_i$ for all $i \le j$.

title: fair_coin_flip_martingale_property
content: A placeholder theorem stating that cumulative sums of fair coin flips form a martingale. If each flip has E[flip] = 0, then the running total has constant expectation regardless of when we stop. This serves as a motivating example for the general theory rather than a formal proof.
mathContext: If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $E[X_i] = 0$, then $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is a martingale: $E[S_{n+1} \mid S_1, \ldots, S_n] = S_n + E[X_{n+1}] = S_n$.

title: isValidStoppingStrategy: Stopping Times
content: Wraps Mathlib's MeasureTheory.IsStoppingTime. A stopping time tau is a random variable where the event {tau <= n} is F_n-measurable: at each moment, we can determine whether we have stopped using only information available at that time. Valid examples include 'first time wealth exceeds $100'; invalid examples include 'the time just before a losing bet' (requires future knowledge).
mathContext: A stopping time $\tau$ with respect to filtration $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies $\{\tau \le n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$ for all $n$. This ensures the decision to stop depends only on observed information.

title: isBoundedStoppingTime
content: A stopping time tau is bounded by N if tau(omega) <= N for all omega. This is the crucial finiteness condition for the Optional Stopping Theorem: it prevents 'play until you win' strategies that would require infinite time. Without boundedness, the conclusion E[X_tau] = E[X_0] can fail even for martingales.
mathContext: A bounded stopping time satisfies $\tau(\omega) \le N$ for all $\omega$ and some fixed $N \in \mathbb{N}$. This ensures the game terminates in finite time and allows application of dominated convergence.

title: stoppedValue': Process at Random Time
content: Defines stoppedValue' X tau omega = X(tau(omega), omega), the value of the stochastic process at the random stopping time. For a gambler, this is their final wealth when they quit. This is a simplified version of Mathlib's MeasureTheory.stoppedValue used in fair_games_theorem_stoppedValue.
mathContext: The stopped value $X_\tau(\omega) = X(\tau(\omega), \omega)$ evaluates the process at the random time $\tau$. The Fair Games Theorem states $E[X_\tau] = E[X_0]$.

title: fair_games_theorem: The Main Result
content: The central theorem (Wiedijk #62): for a martingale f and bounded stopping times tau <= pi with pi <= N, the expectations are equal: integral of f(tau(omega)) = integral of f(pi(omega)). The proof uses le_antisymm: (1) the submartingale property (hf.submartingale) gives E[f_tau] <= E[f_pi] via Mathlib's expected_stoppedValue_mono, and (2) the supermartingale property (hf.supermartingale.neg gives a submartingale of -f) yields E[f_tau] >= E[f_pi] after negation and linarith.
mathContext:
For a martingale $f$ and bounded stopping times $\tau \le \pi \le N$:
$$\int f(\tau(\omega))\, d\mu = \int f(\pi(\omega))\, d\mu$$
Proved by $\le$ (submartingale) and $\ge$ (supermartingale via $-f$) giving equality by antisymmetry.

title: fair_games_corollary: E[X_tau] = E[X_0]
content: The intuitive corollary of the main theorem: for any bounded stopping time tau, E[f_tau] = E[f_0]. Starting with expected value E[X_0], no stopping strategy can improve upon this expectation. The proof applies fair_games_theorem with the constant stopping time tau_0 = 0 (trivially bounded and <= tau) and uses symmetry.
mathContext:
For a martingale $f$ and bounded stopping time $\tau \le N$:
$$\int f(\tau(\omega))\, d\mu = \int f(0, \omega)\, d\mu$$
This is the statement 'you cannot beat a fair game': $E[X_\tau] = E[X_0]$.

title: fair_games_theorem_stoppedValue: Mathlib Notation
content: An alternative formulation of the Fair Games Theorem using Mathlib's MeasureTheory.stoppedValue notation. Since stoppedValue f tau omega = f(tau(omega), omega) by definition, the proof simply unfolds stoppedValue and applies fair_games_theorem. This provides compatibility with other Mathlib results that use the stoppedValue API.
mathContext: Using Mathlib's notation: $\int (\text{stoppedValue}\; f\; \tau)(\omega)\, d\mu = \int (\text{stoppedValue}\; f\; \pi)(\omega)\, d\mu$ where $\text{stoppedValue}\; f\; \tau\; \omega := f(\tau(\omega), \omega)$.

title: submartingale_of_stoppedValue_mono
content: Axiom stating the converse direction of the submartingale characterization: if stopped expectations are monotone for all bounded stopping time pairs tau <= pi, then f is a submartingale. This direction requires deep measure-theoretic arguments to recover the local conditional expectation inequality E[f_{n+1} | F_n] >= f_n from the global monotonicity of stopped values. Axiomatized because the proof involves constructing specific indicator-based stopping times to localize the global property.
mathContext: If $f$ is adapted, integrable, and $\int f(\tau) \le \int f(\pi)$ for all bounded stopping times $\tau \le \pi$, then $f$ is a submartingale: $E[f_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \ge f_n$ a.s.

title: submartingale_characterization: The Iff Theorem
content: Proves the full characterization: a process f (adapted and integrable) is a submartingale if and only if E[f_tau] <= E[f_pi] for all bounded stopping times tau <= pi. The forward direction uses Mathlib's Submartingale.expected_stoppedValue_mono; the converse invokes the submartingale_of_stoppedValue_mono axiom. This connects the local conditional-expectation property to the global stopped-value monotonicity.
mathContext:
For adapted, integrable $f$:
$$f \text{ is a submartingale} \iff \forall\, \tau \le \pi \le N,\; \int f(\tau)\, d\mu \le \int f(\pi)\, d\mu$$
This is the content of Mathlib's submartingale_iff_expected_stoppedValue_mono.

title: martingale_equality_characterization
content: For martingales, the submartingale characterization becomes an equality: E[f_tau] = E[f_pi] for all bounded stopping times tau <= pi. This is a direct application of fair_games_theorem, lifting it to a universal quantifier over all stopping time pairs. It establishes that equality of stopped expectations is the defining global property of martingales.
mathContext:
For a martingale $f$:
$$\forall\, \tau \le \pi \le N,\; \int f(\tau)\, d\mu = \int f(\pi)\, d\mu$$
Martingales are characterized by equality (not just inequality) of stopped expectations.

title: gamblers_ruin_fair_game
content: Application of the Fair Games Theorem to gambler's ruin. A gambler with initial wealth W_0 playing fair coin flips targets W_0 + a before hitting 0. Since E[W_tau] = W_0 and the game ends at either W_0 + a or 0, we get p(W_0 + a) + (1-p)(0) = W_0, yielding P(success) = W_0/(W_0 + a). With W_0 = 10 and target 20, the probability of doubling before ruin is exactly 50%.
mathContext: From $E[W_\tau] = W_0$: if the game ends at $W_0 + a$ with probability $p$ or at $0$ with probability $1-p$, then $p(W_0 + a) = W_0$, so $P(\text{success}) = \frac{W_0}{W_0 + a}$.

title: betting_systems_fail
content: Demonstrates that all betting systems (martingale doubling, D'Alembert, Fibonacci) fail against fair games with bounded play. Under any bounded stopping time, E[final wealth] = E[initial wealth]. Systems that require unbounded time (e.g., 'double until you win') have infinite expected play time and are not implementable with finite bankrolls or time limits.
mathContext: For any betting system implementable as a bounded stopping time $\tau \le N$: $E[W_\tau] = E[W_0]$. The martingale system requires $\tau$ unbounded (exponential bets), so $E[\text{bets needed}] = \infty$.

title: option_pricing_martingale
content: Application to mathematical finance: under the risk-neutral measure Q, discounted asset prices form a martingale. The Fair Games Theorem then justifies pricing derivatives as expected discounted payoffs: the price of an option is E^Q[discounted payoff]. For American options, the optimal exercise time is a stopping time problem, and the Optional Stopping Theorem ensures the price is consistent across exercise strategies.
mathContext: Under the risk-neutral measure $Q$: $E^Q[e^{-rT}S_T \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = e^{-rt}S_t$ (discounted prices are $Q$-martingales). Option price $= E^Q[e^{-r\tau}\text{payoff}(S_\tau)]$ for exercise time $\tau$.

title: doobs_inequality_statement
content: States Doob's maximal inequality: for a non-negative submartingale f, P(max_{n<=N} f_n >= lambda) <= E[f_N]/lambda. This concentration inequality follows from optional stopping arguments and controls the probability that a submartingale exceeds any threshold. It is a key tool in proving convergence theorems for martingales.
mathContext: Doob's maximal inequality: $P\left(\max_{n \le N} f_n \ge \lambda\right) \le \frac{E[f_N]}{\lambda}$ for non-negative submartingales $f$ and $\lambda > 0$.

title: Historical Context and Wiedijk #62
content: Summarizes the historical development from Bachelier (1906, applying fair games to finance), through Levy (1934, conditional expectation sequences), Ville (1939, coining 'martingale'), to Doob (1953, proving the Optional Stopping Theorem). The theorem connects three fundamental ideas: fairness (martingale property), strategy (stopping time), and invariance (the theorem itself). As Wiedijk #62, it represents one of the most practically relevant theorems in probability.
mathContext: Doob (1953) proved: for a martingale $(X_n)$ and bounded stopping time $\tau$, $E[X_\tau] = E[X_0]$. Wiedijk lists this as #62 in his 100 greatest theorems.

title: fair_games_summary
content: Summary theorem restating the core message: the Fair Games Theorem (Wiedijk #62) is formalized via the Optional Stopping Theorem from Mathlib. The key requirements are fairness (martingale), valid strategy (stopping time, no future knowledge), and bounded time (game must end). The main Mathlib reference is submartingale_iff_expected_stoppedValue_mono from Mathlib.Probability.Martingale.OptionalStopping.
mathContext: Summary: $E[f_\tau] = E[f_0]$ for martingale $f$ and bounded stopping time $\tau$. Requirements: (1) $f$ is a martingale, (2) $\tau$ is $\mathcal{F}$-stopping time, (3) $\tau \le N$.
